title: Sukhothai
hookLine: the Thai kingdom whose walking Buddha images seem to move

cards: A bronze figure, caught mid-stride. The right heel is just lifting off the ground. One hand is raised, palm out.
The body leans a little, the way a body leans when it is really walking and not posing for anyone. The robe clings to the legs as if a breeze had caught it.
This week has already brought Buddhas carved in rock, sitting, standing and lying down. This one is going somewhere.
Sculptors in an old Thai kingdom made images like this, and people who stand in front of them say the bronze seems to move.

teach.b: First, the place. Sukhothai is the name of a kingdom and its old capital, in what is now Thailand.
Its ruins still stand among trees and ponds: brick temple platforms, stupas, and rows of seated Buddhas, with the walking ones among them.
Its kings supported Theravada monks, the same stream of teaching that reached Sri Lanka and Myanmar. Second, the story people see in the stride.
Tradition tells that the Buddha once spent a rainy season in Tavatimsa heaven, teaching his mother, who had died soon after his birth.

When the season ended, he came back down to earth by a stairway, with crowds waiting at the bottom. Some readers see that very moment in the walking image: the Buddha stepping down to meet people again.
Third, walking was practice, not just travel. In the old suttas, monks pace back and forth on a short path, and the Buddha walks it too. The Pali word is cankama, walking up and down.

One discourse praises it in plain terms: it helps you bear long journeys, it helps your food digest, and the calm you find while walking tends to last. Fourth, the face. On a walking Buddha it is not hurrying.

teach.h: A QUIET FACE ON A MOVING BODY.
teach.b: The body moves; the face stays quiet: a mind that can stay still while the feet keep going.
A day is full of moving, from the bed to the kettle, from the door to the bus. Sukhothai's bronze makes a claim about all of it: calm doesn't wait for you to sit down.

how: In Theravada monasteries, monks and lay meditators often practice walking meditation, pacing slowly along a short path, and walking Buddha images in the Sukhothai style are still made and honored in Thailand.

games.q: you're a sculptor in Sukhothai, asked to cast a Buddha unlike the seated ones around you. how do you show him?
o: seated, hands in his lap, eyes closed.
mid-stride, heel lifting, one hand raised.
lying on his side at the very end.
games.why: Sukhothai's sculptors cast him walking. the body moves, but the face stays quiet, and tradition links the stride to his return from Tavatimsa heaven.

practice: Find a few steps of clear floor, or if you can't walk right now, rest your hands on your knees and do it in your mind.
Lift one heel slowly, feel the weight roll forward, let the foot touch down, then the other, and at the end of your short path pause, turn and come back, arms loose and face soft like the bronze.

wordCard.voice: Sukhothai. The old Thai kingdom whose sculptors cast the Buddha walking, heel lifting, face at rest. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: walking up and down, the walking practice monks do in the suttas.

carryVoice: Your line: the walking Buddha. The feet keep going; the face stays quiet. That's day eight hundred eighty-seven.
